passage:
Amma pulled a crumpled paper from the bottom of Jahnavi's bag. "Science test. Nineteen out of twenty? Why is this crushed like a peanut wrapper?"
Jahnavi, ten, kept her eyes on her rice. "No reason."
"Last month you stuck your prize certificate on the fridge."
"I took it down."
"I noticed. Why?"
A long pause. "Rafiq and them call me Show-off Jahnavi now. Every time Ma'am reads the marks, they go 'ooooh' and clap slowly."
"So you hide your papers."
"If nobody sees, they forget. Yesterday I said I got twelve. They let me sit with them."
Amma sat down beside her. "And how did twelve feel?"
Jahnavi shrugged, and her eyes filled.

qa.q: What mark did Jahnavi get in the science test?
qa.a: Nineteen out of twenty.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi want when claiming to have got twelve?
qa.a: Jahnavi wanted to be accepted again and sit with the group without being called a show-off.

qa.q: Amma's question "And how did twelve feel?" opens a door. What could Amma do next?
qa.a: Amma could listen to how hurt and lonely Jahnavi feels, and then speak with the class teacher about the slow clapping, rather than just telling Jahnavi to be proud.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see the "ooooh" and the slow clapping?
qa.a: Rafiq may think it is just a joke and not see how much it hurts, or may feel a little envious of Jahnavi's marks.

grounding: A girl who won a prize hides her good marks after classmates mock her as a show-off.

passage: I'm Kamal, and in Class 6 I won the district maths prize. The headmaster read my name at assembly, and I felt tall for about one morning. By lunch, the kids at my table were saying, "Oh, Professor Kamal, please solve my tiffin," and bowing. Someone wrote SHOW-OFF on my desk in chalk. So I changed. When tests came back, I folded mine face down. When Sir asked who got full marks, I kept my hand in my lap. Only Rukmini noticed. "You used to be proud," she said. I told her I didn't care about marks. That wasn't true. I just cared more about lunch.

qa.q: What was written on Kamal's desk in chalk?
qa.a: SHOW-OFF.

qa.q: What does "I just cared more about lunch" reveal about Kamal's feelings?
qa.a: It shows Kamal still valued the marks but feared being left out at lunch even more.

qa.q: Rukmini's comment was a chance to open up. What could Kamal have done then?
qa.a: Kamal could have admitted the teasing hurt and asked Rukmini, or a teacher, for help, instead of pretending not to care.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel watching Kamal fold tests face down?
qa.a: Rukmini seems to miss the proud friend Kamal used to be, and may feel sad that the teasing made Kamal hide. 😔

grounding: A child who won a maths prize is mocked as a show-off and starts hiding test results to fit in.

passage: Note for the file and for the parents of Shankar (Class 5). Since Shankar won the school essay prize last month, I have noticed a change. Classmates started calling him 'show-off' and 'teacher's pet', mostly at recess. This week his essay was half a page, flat, with spelling mistakes in words he spelled correctly in September. When I returned it, he looked relieved at the low grade and showed it to the boys at his table. I spoke to him privately. He said, 'If I'm bad, they'll stop.' Plan: talk to the class about teasing without naming him, praise effort for everyone rather than only toppers, and meet his parents on Friday. — Lokesh Iyer, class teacher

qa.q: Which prize did Shankar win last month?
qa.a: The school essay prize.

qa.q: Why did Shankar look relieved at the low grade?
qa.a: Shankar hoped a poor grade would stop the teasing, believing that being bad would make the others stop.

qa.q: Which part of Lokesh Iyer's plan might help Shankar most, and why?
qa.a: Praising effort for everyone, not only toppers, could make doing well feel less like standing apart, so classmates stop treating Shankar as a target.

qa.q: How might Shankar's parents feel on reading this note?
qa.a: They may be surprised and worried that their child is hiding real ability, and grateful the teacher noticed early.

grounding: A teacher notices a prize-winning boy deliberately writing badly after classmates mock him as a show-off.

subtype: Downplaying own success to stay liked [Actor]
passage:
Dear Raghav Bhaiya,
Don't tell Amma I'm telling you this first. I got selected for the national astronomy camp. Only twelve students from our state. When the list came out, Ma'am wanted to announce it in assembly, and I begged her not to.
In class, when someone asked, I laughed and said, 'They probably mixed up my roll number.' Everyone laughed too. It felt safer than saying I'm thrilled. Because I am. I've wanted this since I was nine.
But you remember what happened to Sreeja when she topped the boards? The whole group started calling her Madam Genius and stopped saving her a seat. I don't want to be Madam Genius.
Is it stupid to hide something this good?
Vidya

qa.q: How many students from the state were selected for the camp?
qa.a: Only twelve students.

qa.q: What was Vidya afraid of when joking about the roll number?
qa.a: Vidya feared that showing pride would make friends turn cold, as they did with Sreeja, and wanted to stay one of the group.

qa.q: Vidya asks whether hiding it is stupid. What first step could Raghav Bhaiya suggest?
qa.a: Raghav Bhaiya could suggest telling one close friend honestly how excited Vidya is and seeing how they react, instead of joking it away with everyone.

qa.q: How might Raghav Bhaiya feel on learning Vidya told him first?
qa.a: Raghav Bhaiya might feel trusted and proud, and also sad that Vidya can't celebrate openly at school. 🙂

grounding: A teenager selected for a national camp jokes it away in class, afraid friends will call them arrogant.

subtype: Downplaying own success to stay liked [Actor]
passage: Okay Parul, since you asked why I went weird in March. Promise not to laugh. I got picked for the national debating championship. Me, Vasudha, from our tiny school. When the club teacher said it in class, I jumped in before anyone could clap: 'Only because the good speakers had exams.' Not true. I won three rounds to get there. I even joked that I'd faint on stage. Everyone laughed and moved on, and I felt this strange relief. Because last year, when Kunal got into the state team, people started saying he'd 'changed' and 'thinks he's too good for us.' I was scared that would be me. So I shrank it. Silly, right? Anyway, I lost in the quarterfinals. I didn't even tell you that.

qa.q: How many rounds did Vasudha win to get to the championship?
qa.a: Three rounds.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha feel relief when everyone laughed and moved on?
qa.a: Vasudha feared being seen as someone who had 'changed', like Kunal, so shrinking the news felt safe even though it wasn't true.

qa.q: In the classroom moment, what different choice could Vasudha have made?
qa.a: When the teacher announced it, Vasudha could have simply said thank you and let people clap, trusting real friends to be glad.

qa.q: What might Parul feel on hearing all this months later?
qa.a: Parul might feel hurt at being left out of both the win and the loss, and sad that Vasudha expected a friend to turn cold.

grounding: A teenager picked for a national debating event jokes it away, afraid classmates will say they have changed.

subtype: Downplaying own success to stay liked [Actor]
passage: I sit behind Rukmini in Class 11, so I saw her face when the sports teacher read out the national under-17 football camp list. Her name was the only one from our school. For a second she lit up, properly lit up. Then she turned round and said, loud enough for the back bench, 'They needed a goalkeeper who's good at falling down.' People laughed. At lunch someone asked about the camp, and she said it was 'just some practice thing.' She kept her new camp kit in a plastic bag instead of wearing it. I don't know exactly what she was feeling. But last year, when a girl from 11B got into the state squad, a few people called her 'Miss Big Shot' for months. Maybe Rukmini remembered too. — Aparna

qa.a: Rukmini's name was the only one.

qa.q: What might Rukmini's quick change from lighting up to joking suggest?

qa.a: Aparna could say something warm, like how great the selection is, so Rukmini feels safe to be proud without the group turning cold.

qa.q: How does the camp news look from Aparna's seat?
qa.a: From behind, Aparna sees both the brief joy and the joke, and suspects Rukmini is hiding pride out of fear, though Aparna can't be sure.

grounding: A classmate watches a girl selected for a national camp joke it away, possibly afraid of being called arrogant.

passage: In the architecture studio, Professor Menon stopped at Gautam's model and actually smiled. "Look at this light well, everyone. This is how you think about a courtyard." Twenty students crowded round. Jaya stood at the back. It was good; she could see that. The folded roof, the way the light fell. Something tightened under her ribs. "The glue's showing at the corners," she said, a little too loud. "And the scale figures are wrong. Those people would be three metres tall." A few people laughed. Gautam's ears went red. Later, back at her own desk, Jaya stared at her plain box of a model. She had spent the same three weeks. Why did his look like that? She peeled a strip of tape off her roof, then pressed it back.

qa.q: What did Jaya say about the scale figures?
qa.a: That they were wrong and those people would be three metres tall.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when something tightened under her ribs?
qa.a: Jaya admired the model but felt a sting of envy and fear of falling behind, which came out as criticism.

qa.q: What could Jaya do the next time that tight feeling comes, instead of pointing out faults?
qa.a: Jaya could notice the feeling, admit the work is good, and perhaps ask Gautam how the light well was designed.

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt when the others laughed?
qa.a: Gautam's red ears suggest embarrassment; a moment of praise was spoiled by a classmate's public nitpicking.

grounding: A student feels envy when a classmate's model is praised and publicly picks small faults in it.

passage:
Hi Rehana,
Big news from college: Harleen got the Tokyo exchange scholarship. Everyone's congratulating her like she cured something.
Honestly? Her essay wasn't that great. I read it; she used 'passionate' four times. And she only got the interview because Professor Bhalla likes her. Also, she can't even use chopsticks properly, which is funny for someone going to Japan.
I applied too, you know. I didn't tell anyone. The rejection mail came the same morning the list went up.
I know I sound petty. I used to think Harleen was the most interesting person in our batch. I still sort of do. That's what's annoying.
Anyway, how's Pune?
Jyoti

qa.q: What feelings show when Jyoti writes "That's what's annoying"?

qa.a: Rehana may see past the jokes to a friend hurt by a quiet rejection, and might gently ask about it.

passage: You know what I did last week, Salma? I'm not proud of it. At the call centre, the team lead put Deepa's name on the board, 'Agent of the Month,' with a gold star. Deepa joined after me. Everyone clapped, and I clapped too, but my face felt hot. Then at tea break I said, 'Well, she takes the easy calls, no? Billing questions.' And, 'She reads straight off the script.' Small things. Nothing that was even untrue, exactly. But I watched people nod and look at her differently. The thing is, I used to go to Deepa when I got stuck. She's good. I think I was scared that I, Kiran, would be stuck in the same seat forever while she moved up.

subtype: Team sniping at the promoted colleague [Observer]
passage:
"Why is the sprint board half empty?" Ojas asked, stopping at Trisha's desk.
"Nobody's picked up tasks since Monday." Trisha kept her voice low. "I asked in the channel. Three thumbs-up, zero names."
"Since your promotion was announced."
"You noticed too."
Across the aisle, Varun laughed. "Ask the team lead. She knows everything now."
Ojas turned. "Varun, a minute?"
In the pantry, Varun shrugged. "We were all equals last month. Now she assigns my work. It's weird, man."
"Weird isn't the same as wrong."
"I'm not doing anything."
"That's the problem," Ojas said quietly. "Nobody's doing anything. Let's talk about how to make this work for all of you."

qa.q: How many thumbs-up did Trisha get in the channel?
qa.a: Three thumbs-up, zero names.

qa.q: What is Varun feeling beneath "It's weird"?
qa.a: Varun seems uneasy that a former equal now assigns the work, and some resentment shows in the jab that she knows everything now.

qa.q: What choice does Ojas make with Varun, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: Ojas talks to Varun privately, names the quiet withdrawal without shaming, and offers to work out how the new setup can suit everyone.

qa.q: What is it like for Trisha to lead a team that has gone quiet?
qa.a: Trisha must feel isolated and unsure, with colleagues who were equals last month now leaving the board empty.

subtype: Team sniping at the promoted colleague [Observer]
passage: I'm Lalit, and I've managed the Nashik branch accounts team for four years. Last spring I promoted Santosh to senior. He'd earned it. What I didn't expect was how fast the room changed. The team's chat group, which used to buzz with jokes, went quiet whenever Santosh posted. His lunch table emptied; people suddenly had 'errands.' When he asked for the monthly reports, they came in exactly on the deadline, never early like before. Nobody was rude. That was what made it hard to name. Looking back, I think the team had been comfortable as equals, all grumbling about the same things, and Santosh moving up broke that. I should have talked to them sooner instead of hoping it would settle.

qa.q: How long has Lalit managed the Nashik branch accounts team?
qa.a: Four years.

qa.q: What does Lalit feel looking back?
qa.a: Lalit feels some regret for waiting and hoping it would settle instead of talking to the team sooner.

qa.q: What could Lalit have done in the first weeks after the promotion?
qa.a: Lalit could have met the team to talk openly about the change and how roles would work, and checked in with Santosh privately.

passage: When Liam's email arrived, Tariq was eating toast over the sink in their Manchester flat: My first solo exhibition! Opening Friday. Tariq read it twice. He and Liam had started painting at the same evening class. Tariq had stopped after six months, busy with overtime. He picked the phone up again and wrote: Mate, that's brilliant. I'll be there Friday. Proud of you. Then, after a moment: Can I buy you a coffee after and hear how you found the time? He sent it, and pulled out the box under his bed where his paints still were.

"Congratulations. Genuinely. Can I ask what you did to get it?" Chetan blinked, then grinned. "Coffee? I'll tell you what I'd do if I were you."

passage:
Dear Akash,
I owe you a proper note, not just the thumbs-up I sent in the group.
When you told us your short story was accepted by the literary magazine, my first feeling wasn't joy. It was a pinch. We started writing together in college, and I've had eleven rejections this year. For a day I caught myself thinking your ending was rushed. It wasn't. It's beautiful.
So: congratulations. Really. I'm proud to know you.
And the pinch told me something useful. I've been writing less and complaining more. I want what you have, so I'm going to write every morning this month.
Would you read my next draft, when it's ready?
Aparna

qa.q: How many rejections has Aparna had this year?
qa.a: Eleven rejections.

qa.q: What was Aparna's first feeling about Akash's news, and why?
qa.a: A pinch of envy rather than joy, because they started writing together and Aparna has had many rejections.

qa.q: What choice did Aparna make with that pinch of envy?
qa.a: Aparna named it, congratulated Akash properly, and used it as a sign to write every morning this month.

qa.q: What might this honest note mean to Akash?
qa.a: Akash may feel moved by the honesty and trusted as a friend, and glad the success is celebrated rather than resented. ❤️

grounding: A young adult owns envy at a friend's publication, congratulates the friend, and turns it into a personal writing goal.

passage:
"Aunty Elizabeth's going to sing that song again," Baljeet groaned, flopping on the bed while the cousins set up for Nani's birthday. "The one that sounds like a sad goat."
"It's a Welsh lullaby," said his cousin Simran. "She sang it at the wedding, at Lohri, at Diwali…"
"Exactly. Every. Single. Time."
That night, in the crowded living room, Aunty Elizabeth sang with her eyes closed. Baljeet mouthed the words before he could stop himself.
Simran nudged him. "You know it!"
"No I don't."
"You're humming, Baljeet."
He was. Later, brushing his teeth, he hummed it again, slower. It didn't sound like a goat any more. It sounded like Nani's house.

qa.a: At the wedding, at Lohri, at Diwali.

qa.q: What does Baljeet's humming while brushing his teeth suggest?

qa.a: Aunty Elizabeth would probably feel touched and welcome, seeing her song become part of the family's gatherings.

passage: I'm Vikas, and when I was eight I thought the song Deepak Chacha played at every family function was the worst thing ever. It was a slow old film song with a long, wobbly violin bit, and the singer held the notes forever. At Bua's wedding I put my fingers in my ears. At my cousin's mundan, I groaned. At Dadi's birthday I rolled my eyes so hard Mummy pinched me. But by the fourth or fifth time, something changed. I started waiting for the violin part. Then one day at school I caught myself whistling it in the lunch line. Now, whenever I hear it, I think of samosas and cousins.

qa.a: Vikas put fingers in the ears.

qa.q: How did Vikas's feelings about the song change, and what shows it?
qa.a: Vikas went from disliking it to looking forward to it, shown by waiting for the violin part and whistling it at school.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vikas's feelings, and what does it suggest for the next strange song Vikas hears?
qa.a: Around the fourth or fifth hearing, Vikas began waiting for the violin part; next time, Vikas could give a strange song a few more listens before deciding.

qa.q: How might Deepak Chacha feel hearing Vikas whistle the song?
qa.a: Deepak Chacha would probably be delighted, since the song finally reached a child who once groaned at it.

subtype: Warming to a classmate through daily contact [Actor]
passage: On the first day, Rehana decided she did not like the new girl. Zainab laughed too loudly on the school bus, wore her braid over one shoulder like a film heroine, and took the window seat that had been Rehana's for two years. In Mumbai traffic, the ride took forty minutes. Every morning Zainab got on at Kurla, sat next to Rehana, and opened a tin of her mother's parathas. By the second week Rehana knew which stop made Zainab sigh (the cement works) and which made her smile (the bakery). By the fourth week they were splitting parathas. In class, when Zainab got the maths wrong, Rehana found herself whispering the answer. She wasn't sure when that had happened.

qa.q: How long did the bus ride take in Mumbai traffic?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What does Rehana whispering the maths answer suggest about her feelings now?
qa.a: It shows Rehana has quietly started to care about Zainab, without even noticing the change.

qa.a: Rehana could say something friendly out loud, maybe ask Zainab to sit together at lunch, and admit the first impression was too quick.

qa.q: How might Zainab have experienced the first few weeks on the bus?
qa.a: Zainab, new at the school, may have felt Rehana's coolness but kept sharing the tin, perhaps hoping to make a friend.

subtype: Warming to a classmate through daily contact [Actor]
passage:
"You're late," Himani said as Pallavi ran up to the bus stop, dripping.
"You saved my spot?"
"No. The spot saved itself." Himani shifted her umbrella over both of them anyway.
Pallavi grinned. "Six weeks ago you wouldn't even look at me."
"Six weeks ago you told me my handwriting looked like ants fighting."
"It does."
"See? That's why."
"And now?"
Himani shrugged. "Now I'm used to you, I suppose. Same bus, same bench, same chemistry partner. You grow on people. Like mould."
"Wow. Thank you."
The bus came round the corner. Pallavi reached for the rail, then turned. "Sit with me?"
"Obviously," Himani said, and was surprised to find she meant it.

qa.q: What did Pallavi say about Himani's handwriting six weeks ago?
qa.a: That it looked like ants fighting.

qa.q: What does Himani feel on being surprised to mean "Obviously"?
qa.a: Himani is surprised to find a real liking for Pallavi now, after starting out annoyed.

qa.q: Which small choice at the bus stop shows Himani warming up, and what could come next?
qa.a: Sharing the umbrella and agreeing to sit together show it; next, Himani could tell Pallavi plainly that the friendship matters.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel hearing "You grow on people"?
qa.a: Pallavi seems amused and pleased, reading the teasing as a sign that Himani now enjoys Pallavi's company. 😊

grounding: A teenager who was put off by a new classmate grows to like that classmate through daily bus rides and lessons together.

subtype: Warming to a classmate through daily contact [Actor]
passage: My name's Noor, and in Class 10 a boy called Thomas joined our section in the middle of term. I didn't like him. He answered every question, he tapped his pen, and he had a laugh like a bicycle horn. Our roll numbers put us on the same bench for every exam and every lab. Then his family moved into our building, so we were in the same school van too. Twice a day, every day. I can't point to the day it changed. Maybe it was when he lent me his calculator without being asked, or when I worked out that his pen-tapping meant he was nervous. By December I was saving him a seat in the van. Being near him so much just wore the dislike away.

qa.q: What did Thomas's laugh sound like to Noor?
qa.a: Like a bicycle horn.

qa.q: What did Noor come to understand about the pen-tapping, and how did that change Noor's feelings?
qa.a: Noor worked out that it meant Thomas was nervous, which made the habit feel less annoying and more human.

qa.q: Noor started saving Thomas a seat in December. Why was that choice significant?
qa.a: It turned Noor's quiet change of feeling into a friendly act that Thomas could see.

qa.q: How might Thomas have experienced joining in the middle of term?
qa.a: Joining mid-term, Thomas may have felt nervous, as the pen-tapping suggests, and grateful for any friendliness from a bench partner.

grounding: A teenager who disliked a new classmate grows to like him after seeing him daily on the same bench and van.

subtype: Familiar brand mistaken for a better one [Actor]
passage: Sit, Zeenat. Let your Tanuja Aunty tell you about her first pressure cooker. I was twenty, just married, and I went to the market with my own money for the first time. There were six on the shelf. One brand had been on the radio every morning of my life, a jingle I could sing in my sleep. I picked it without lifting the others. Paid almost double. The shopkeeper said the plain steel one beside it was thicker and had a better valve. I told him, 'Everyone knows this name.' Knowing a name, I learned later, is not the same as knowing a thing. That cooker's handle broke in a year. My neighbour's plain one is still whistling. So when you choose your laptop, beta, lift the other ones too.

qa.q: How much more did Tanuja Aunty pay for the famous cooker?
qa.a: Almost double.

qa.q: Why was Tanuja Aunty so sure about the famous cooker at twenty?
qa.a: The jingle had played every morning for years, so the name felt trustworthy; familiarity felt like quality.

qa.q: What could Tanuja Aunty have done when the shopkeeper spoke up?
qa.a: Tanuja Aunty could have lifted the plain steel one and compared its thickness and valve, instead of trusting the familiar name.

qa.q: What might Zeenat take from the story when choosing a laptop?
qa.a: Zeenat may realise that a name heard everywhere isn't proof of quality, and compare the less famous options too.

grounding: An elder recalls buying a heavily advertised cooker at twenty because the name felt familiar, not because it was better.

subtype: Familiar brand mistaken for a better one [Actor]
passage: Their train left in six minutes, and Jyoti's phone was at four percent. The station stall had three power banks hanging on hooks. One was from the company whose ads played before every video Jyoti watched, a bright orange box she'd seen a thousand times. "That one," she said, already pulling out cash. Zainab, hauling both suitcases, glanced at the others. "That grey one has a bigger capacity and it's cheaper." "Never heard of it." "Does that make it worse?" The whistle blew. Jyoti grabbed the orange one and ran. On the train she read the box properly: half the capacity of the grey one, at a price that would have covered lunch. It still felt like the safe choice. She wasn't sure why.

qa.q: How many power banks were hanging at the stall?
qa.a: Three power banks.

qa.q: Why did the orange one still feel like the safe choice, even after Jyoti read the box?
qa.a: Jyoti had seen it a thousand times in ads, so it felt trusted and familiar, even though the grey one was better on paper.

qa.a: Jyoti could have compared capacity and price on the boxes, as Zainab did, which would have taken seconds.

qa.a: Zainab might feel a bit exasperated after pointing out the better, cheaper option, but also understand the rush. 😅

subtype: Familiar brand mistaken for a better one [Actor]
passage: The sports shop on Brigade Road had a whole wall of running shoes. Tejas walked straight to the pair whose logo he'd seen on hoardings at every signal and on cricket shirts on TV. "These," he told the salesman. "Size nine." Hrithik picked up a plain blue pair from the lower shelf. "Try these too. They're lighter." "I've never heard of that company." "You've never heard of most things. Just try them." Tejas tried both. The blue ones were softer, honestly. But the famous ones felt… right. Like something he already owned. He paid for the famous ones, nearly twice as much. Three weeks later, on his morning run, the blister on his heel told him what his feet had known in the shop.

qa.q: What did Hrithik pick up from the lower shelf?
qa.a: A plain blue pair.

qa.q: What did Tejas feel when the famous shoes seemed like something already owned?
qa.a: Tejas had seen the logo so often that the shoes felt familiar and safe, and that comfort was mistaken for quality.

qa.q: At which moment could Tejas have chosen differently, and what should have guided the choice?
qa.a: After trying both, Tejas could have gone with the softer blue pair, trusting the feel on his feet over the familiar logo.

qa.q: How might Hrithik react on hearing about the blister?
qa.a: Hrithik might tease Tejas a little, but also feel sorry, having suggested the lighter pair in the shop.

grounding: A young man buys the running shoes he knows from ads despite finding a plain pair more comfortable.

passage: It was the last week of the month, and Raghav had exactly six hundred rupees until salary day. For three months in Kolkata he'd eaten the same rajma-chawal at the same dhaba near the office. Safe. Known. Last night his colleague Hemant had laughed: "You live in the city of fish and you eat rajma?" Raghav had wanted to argue that he just liked rajma. Then he wondered: did he, or was it just the only thing he knew here? So he made a rule. Three tries, sixty rupees each, before deciding. Monday: shukto from a steel-plate canteen, bitter and strange. Wednesday: mustard fish, bony, but the sauce… Friday he went back for the fish on his own.

qa.q: How much money did Raghav have until salary day?
qa.a: Exactly six hundred rupees.

qa.q: What doubt made Raghav want to test his taste?
qa.a: Raghav wondered whether he truly liked rajma or only liked it because it was the one thing he knew in the city.

qa.q: Why was Raghav's three-tries rule a good choice with little money?
qa.a: It kept each try cheap, at sixty rupees, and gave unfamiliar food a fair chance instead of judging it on one strange first bite.

qa.q: How might Hemant react to seeing Raghav order mustard fish on his own?
qa.a: Hemant would probably be amused and pleased, since the teasing nudged Raghav toward a new favourite.

grounding: An adult suspects his fondness for one dish is just familiarity and gives local food three cheap, fair tries.

passage: For six years Suraj had ridden the metro to Noida with the same forty songs in his ears. When his flatmate Wasim played old jazz records on Sunday mornings, Suraj called it 'lift music.' Then one day he noticed something: he'd never actually listened to it. He'd only decided. And those forty songs, he loved them, but hadn't he first heard most of them on repeat in a college hostel? Maybe loving them was mostly knowing them. So he asked Wasim for three recordings and promised to give each one five full listens on his commute, no skipping. By the third day, the second piece had a phrase he kept waiting for. He didn't love it yet. But he'd stopped calling it lift music.

qa.q: How many songs did Suraj play on the commute?
qa.a: The same forty songs.

qa.q: What did Suraj start to think about loving those forty songs?
qa.a: Suraj suspected the love was mostly familiarity from hearing them on repeat in a college hostel, not a fair judgment.

qa.q: What made Suraj's plan with Wasim's recordings a fair test?
qa.a: Five full listens each, with no skipping, gave the new music the same repeated exposure the old songs had enjoyed.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel when Suraj asks for recordings?
qa.a: Wasim might feel pleased and a little surprised, since Suraj had dismissed the music, and happy to share something loved.

grounding: An adult realises his music taste may be mostly familiarity and gives his flatmate's jazz several fair listens.

passage:
"Bhabhi, can I help?" Bhupen leaned into the kitchen doorway.
Alka looked up from the dough, surprised. "You? You've avoided this kitchen since the wedding."
"I know." He rubbed his neck. "Honestly, I think I just wasn't used to you. Five months, and I kept thinking, she's so different, she laughs so loud, her food's too sweet."
"Too sweet?"
"Was. I tried your dal three times this week, properly, not just a spoon. Third time, I finished the bowl."
Alka laughed, loud as ever. "So now I'm allowed?"
"I'm giving it a fair chance. You, the food, the music you play in the evening. Two weeks, no complaining."
She handed him a rolling pin. "Start with this, then."

qa.q: How many times did Bhupen try Alka's dal this week?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What did Bhupen realise about the early dislike of Alka?
qa.a: Bhupen realised it came mostly from not being used to someone new, not from anything wrong with Alka.

qa.q: What choice did Bhupen make, and why might it work?
qa.a: Bhupen chose to give Alka, her food and her music a fair two-week chance with no complaining, letting familiarity grow before judging.

qa.q: How might Alka feel when Bhupen offers to help?
qa.a: Alka seems surprised and amused, and may feel relieved and welcomed after five months of being kept at a distance.

grounding: A young man admits his coolness towards his new sister-in-law came from unfamiliarity and gives her, her food and her music a fair try.
